title: Operators and extensions
sub: op_Addition, implicit and explicit, extension methods and C# 14 extension blocks
cards/0/title: An operator is a static method
cards/0/body:
The CLR has no "operator overloading". When you write operator +, the compiler creates an ordinary static method with the special name op_Addition and the specialname flag. The expression a + b becomes call Money::op_Addition(a, b).

C# rules:

  • an operator is public static, and at least one parameter is your type;
  • paired operators are declared together: == with !=, < with >, <= with >=;
  • if you declare ==, override Equals and GetHashCode, or get warnings CS0660/CS0661;
  • += is built from + and an assignment by default.
cards/0/deep:
Names like op_Addition, op_Equality, op_Implicit are reserved by the ECMA-335 standard, and other .NET languages recognize operators by them. A language without operator overloading can call the same method by name.

C# 11 added checked operators (op_CheckedAddition), and C# 14 added user-defined compound assignment: an instance public void operator +=(Money m) named op_AdditionAssignment changes the object in place, without creating a new one. Useful for large buffers and tensors.
cards/1/q: Money is the struct from the example above. What does the compiler turn total += price into?
cards/1/explain: Money has no += operator, so the compiler takes op_Addition and assigns the result. It is a static method: the call instruction, no callvirt. The IL add instruction works only with primitives.
cards/1/wrong/1: Operators are static and called with call: there is no receiver object and no slot.
cards/1/wrong/2: add is for int, double and other CLR primitives. The Money struct is not one of them.
cards/2/title: The operator is chosen at compile time
cards/2/body:
Since an operator is a static method, the compiler chooses it by static types, just like method overloads. No virtual dispatch.

The classic trap is == through object. string has its own op_Equality that compares characters. But if both variables are declared as object, the compiler sees only object == object: a reference comparison.

Same in generics: in a method with where T : class the expression a == b is always a reference comparison, even if T turns out to be string. To compare values use Equals or EqualityComparer<T>.Default.
cards/3/options/2: Does not compile: == is not allowed for T
cards/3/explain: With the class constraint the compiler allows == and binds it to reference comparison: it does not see string op_Equality when compiling the generic. Concat creates a new string, so the references differ.
cards/3/wrong/2: That would be true without the class constraint. With where T : class, == is allowed but compares references.
cards/3/wrong/3: The string from Concat is created at run time and is not interned, so the references differ.
cards/4/body:
User-defined conversions are static methods too: op_Implicit and op_Explicit. The CLR itself allows overloading by return type for any method, but in C# this is the only place where it shows up: one class can have several op_Implicit methods with the same parameter and different results.

  • implicit: the compiler inserts the call itself. Only for conversions that lose no data and never throw.
  • explicit: you have to write (Type)x. For anything that may truncate or fail.

You cannot declare a conversion to or from an interface, to object, to a base class or a derived class: the CLR already has those casts. And remember from the unit "How a type is built": user-defined conversions are not called through object.
cards/5/q: Which declarations inside public class Money compile? Select all.
cards/5/explain: A conversion to object is forbidden: it is a base class (CS0553). To an interface is not allowed either (CS0552). And without static the operator cannot be declared at all.
cards/6/title: Version 2: operators are baked into the calling IL
cards/6/body:
The operator is chosen at compile time and written into the consumer IL as a specific method. Hence two "version 2" scenarios:

  • v2 adds a more precise overload, say Money + decimal. The old consumer keeps calling what the compiler chose earlier: op_Implicit(decimal), then op_Addition(Money, Money). The new overload kicks in only after a recompile.
  • v2 removes an implicit conversion or turns it into explicit. For source code that is a compile error, and for an old consumer it is a MissingMethodException on the first call of a method that used op_Implicit.

An operator signature is as much a part of the public API as a method name.
cards/7/title: An extension method is a static call
cards/7/body:
An extension method is a static method of a static class whose first parameter is marked with this. The compiler puts ExtensionAttribute on it.

The call title.Truncate(10) is syntactic sugar. In IL it is call StringExt::Truncate(title, 10): no callvirt, no null check on the receiver. That is why an extension method can be called on null: an exception happens only if the method itself touches the parameter.

To make the method visible you need a using for the namespace of its class. Remove the using and the method "disappears".
cards/8/q: StringExt from the example above. What happens?
cards/8/options/0: Prints True, then NullReferenceException inside Truncate
cards/8/options/1: NullReferenceException on the very first call
cards/8/options/2: Prints True and an empty string
cards/8/options/3: Does not compile: null has no methods
cards/8/explain: An extension call is a static call; null is simply passed as an argument. IsBlank handles null. Truncate reads s.Length and fails inside the method.
cards/8/wrong/1: That is what an instance method would do: callvirt checks the receiver for null. An extension is called with call.
cards/9/body:
The compiler looks for a method in two stages. First among the instance methods of the type. Only if none is applicable does it look at extensions in visible namespaces.

Note: "applicable" does not mean "a better match". If the type has Log(object), the call x.Log(5) goes there with boxing, even if an extension Log(this X x, int n) with the exact type is right next to it.

Version 2. You wrote a Shuffle extension for someone else's type. In v2 of the library the type gets its own Shuffle(). Your old assembly keeps calling your extension: its IL has a static call. But after a recompile every call silently moves to the library method, without a single warning.
cards/10/explain: item.Show(5): the instance Show(object) is applicable, the int gets boxed to object. Once an applicable instance method is found, extensions are not considered, even though Show(int) is more precise. item.Show() with no arguments does not fit the instance method, so the extension runs. Ext.Show(item, 5) is an explicit static call.
cards/11/body:
C# 14 (.NET 10) introduced extension members. Inside a static class you write an extension(receiver) block, and it can declare more than methods:

  • extension properties: name.IsBlank without parentheses;
  • static members of the type: a block without a receiver name, called as string.Dash;
  • operators for someone else's type.

Old this methods are still here. An instance method in a block compiles to the same IL as a this method, so a library can move to the new syntax without breaking consumers, neither binary nor source.
cards/11/deep:
Blocks have the same restrictions as classic extensions: a top-level, static, non-generic class. Type parameters go on the block itself: extension<T>(IEnumerable<T> source).

The priority has not changed: an instance member of the type still beats an extension. The compiler turns an extension property into a static accessor method with the receiver as the first parameter and adds auxiliary metadata that lets the consumer compiler recognize the block. Extension indexers arrive in the next version, C# 15.
cards/12/q: Declare an extension property in C# 14 style
cards/12/explain: The block extension<T>(List<T> list) declares the receiver for all members inside. this before a parameter is the syntax of classic extension methods; a property cannot be declared that way.
